description: The work is diagnosis and improvisation against buildings that were built wrong forty years ago. Treat it as the technical field it is, and take the small-business side seriously - most of these guests are running a company as well as swinging tools.

questions.text: How much of the job is the physical work, and how much is figuring out what is actually wrong?
questions.lands_because: Reframes the trade as diagnostic work, which is how tradespeople see themselves and how outsiders almost never do. It changes the whole tenor of the interview.
followups: What is the hardest diagnosis you have made?

questions.text: What is the worst thing you have opened up a wall and found?
questions.lands_because: Every tradesperson has this story and enjoys telling it. Perfect early-episode material, and it establishes the improvisation the job requires.
followups: Who did that, and were they licensed?

questions.text: How do you price a job when you cannot know what you will find?
questions.lands_because: Bidding under uncertainty is the central business risk of the trades, and it is a genuinely interesting decision problem that nobody asks about.
followups: When did you last eat a mistake on a bid?

questions.text: What do you see on a job that tells you who worked on it before you, and what they were like?
questions.lands_because: Reading another tradesperson's work is a form of connoisseurship, and hearing it described makes the audience see a building differently forever.
followups: What will the next person say about your work?

questions.text: What is the code requirement you follow that customers fight you on?
questions.lands_because: Puts the guest in the position of the professional defending a standard against pressure, which is both accurate and flattering.
followups: What happens when they go find someone who will?

questions.text: What does this work do to a body over twenty years, and what are you doing about it?
questions.lands_because: The physical cost is universal in the trades and rarely discussed with outsiders. The second clause keeps it from being pitying.
